title: Valence Bond Theory
lead: Valence bond theory describes a covalent bond as the overlap of half-filled atomic orbitals on two atoms, which Lewis structures and VSEPR shapes leave unexplained. The energy of two hydrogen atoms drawn together sets the bond distance and the bond energy, and the two ways orbitals overlap, end to end and side by side, build single, double and triple bonds.
objectives: Describe the formation of covalent bonds in terms of atomic orbital overlap
Define and give examples of σ and π bonds
summary_html: Valence bond theory describes bonding as a consequence of the overlap of two separate atomic orbitals on different atoms that creates a region with one pair of electrons shared between the two atoms. When the orbitals overlap along an axis containing the nuclei, they form a σ bond. When they overlap in a fashion that creates a node along this axis, they form a π bond.

exercises.prompt: Identify each illustration as depicting a σ or π bond: (a) side-by-side overlap of a 4p and a 2p orbital (b) end-to-end overlap of a 4p and 4p orbital (c) end-to-end overlap of a 4p and a 2p orbital

answer.solution: (a) is a π bond with a node along the axis connecting the nuclei while (b) and (c) are σ bonds that overlap along the axis.

exercises.prompt: Explain how σ and π bonds are similar and how they are different.

answer.solution: Similarities: Both types of bonds result from overlap of atomic orbitals on adjacent atoms and contain a maximum of two electrons. Differences: σ bonds are stronger and result from end-to-end overlap and all single bonds are σ bonds; π bonds between the same two atoms are weaker because they result from side-by-side overlap, and multiple bonds contain one or more π bonds (in addition to a σ bond).

exercises.prompt: Explain why bonds occur at specific average bond distances instead of the atoms approaching each other infinitely close.

answer.solution: The specific average bond distance is the distance with the lowest energy. At distances less than the bond distance, the positive charges on the two nuclei repel each other, and the overall energy increases.

exercises.prompt: Use valence bond theory to explain the bonding in F<sub>2</sub>, HF, and ClBr. Sketch the overlap of the atomic orbitals involved in the bonds.

answer.solution: Each bond is a σ bond formed by the end-to-end overlap of two half-filled orbitals, one from each atom, whose single electrons pair. A fluorine atom (1s22s22p5) has one half-filled 2p orbital. In F2 the half-filled 2p orbitals of the two fluorine atoms overlap end to end along the internuclear axis, a p–p σ bond like that of Cl2. In HF the half-filled 1s orbital of hydrogen overlaps the end of the half-filled 2p orbital of fluorine, an s–p σ bond like that of HCl. In ClBr the half-filled 3p orbital of chlorine (3s23p5) overlaps end to end with the half-filled 4p orbital of bromine (4s24p5), another p–p σ bond. The sketches match Figure 8.4: two dumbbell-shaped p orbitals meeting lobe to lobe on the line between the nuclei for F2 and ClBr, with the larger bromine orbital drawn bigger, and a sphere meeting one lobe of a p orbital for HF. In each the overlap region lies on the internuclear axis.

exercises.prompt: Use valence bond theory to explain the bonding in O<sub>2</sub>. Sketch the overlap of the atomic orbitals involved in the bonds in O<sub>2</sub>.

answer.solution: Bonding: One σ bond and one π bond. The s orbitals are filled and do not overlap. The p orbitals overlap along the axis to form a σ bond and side-by-side to form the π bond.

exercises.prompt: How many σ and π bonds are present in the molecule HCN?

answer.solution: HCN has two σ bonds and two π bonds. Its Lewis structure is H–C≡N:, with carbon as the central atom joined to hydrogen by a single bond and to nitrogen by a triple bond, which gives carbon four bonds and nitrogen an octet with one lone pair (10 valence electrons in all). Every bond between two atoms contains one σ bond, so the C–H bond and the C≡N bond give two σ bonds. The second and third lines of the triple bond are π bonds, so there are two π bonds, both between carbon and nitrogen.

exercises.prompt: A friend tells you N2 has three π bonds due to overlap of the three p-orbitals on each N atom. Do you agree?

answer.solution: No, two of the p orbitals (one on each N) will be oriented end-to-end and will form a σ bond.

exercises.prompt:
Draw the Lewis structures for CO<sub>2</sub> and CO, and predict the number of σ and π bonds for each molecule.
(a) CO<sub>2</sub>
(b) CO

answer.solution:
(a) CO2 has two σ bonds and two π bonds. Its 16 valence electrons give the Lewis structure O=C=O, with two lone pairs on each oxygen atom. Each carbon-oxygen double bond is one σ bond and one π bond, so the two double bonds give two of each.
(b) CO has one σ bond and two π bonds. Its 10 valence electrons give the Lewis structure :C≡O:, with one lone pair on each atom, the only arrangement that gives both atoms an octet. The triple bond contains one σ bond, and its second and third lines are two π bonds, as in N2.
